Crunchy foods.Celery: It's about 95 percent water, yet its fibrous strings make it snap loudly. 'Negative calorie' celery is a myth, though it is very low in calories.
Crunchy foods.Crackers: Crackers are named for the crackling sound they make. Early ones, like ship's biscuit, were baked to last for months at sea.
Crunchy foods.Potato chips: Legend says George Crum invented them in 1853, when a customer demanded thinner fries. Food historians doubt the story, but it persists.
Crunchy foods.Croutons: Bread cubes baked or fried until crisp. They're a way to rescue stale bread and add crunch to salads and soups.
Crunchy foods.Carrot sticks: Raw carrot snaps loudly because of its stiff cell walls. Carrots were originally purple or yellow, and orange ones arrived later in Europe.
Crunchy foods.Popcorn: Popcorn pops because its hull traps moisture that turns to steam at around 180 degrees Celsius, bursting the kernel.
Crunchy foods.Pretzels: A pretzel's twist is said to mimic arms crossed in prayer. Their glossy brown crust comes from a lye or baking soda bath before baking.
Crunchy foods.Granola: Invented in the 1800s as a health food. It crunches because oats are baked with sweetener and oil until they dry and clump.
Crunchy foods.Almonds: The almond is actually the seed of a fruit related to peaches. Most of the world's supply comes from California.
Crunchy foods.Tortilla chips: Fried or baked corn tortilla pieces. They were popularized in the 1940s in Los Angeles by a factory that recycled misshapen tortillas.
Crunchy foods.Apple: Apples float because about a quarter of their volume is air, and a fresh one's crunch comes from firm, juicy cells.
Crunchy foods.Biscotti: Italian for 'twice cooked': the loaf is baked, sliced and baked again, which makes it hard and dry for dunking in coffee.
Crunchy foods.Rice cakes: Whole rice grains are puffed under heat and pressure into a disc, then crisped. They crunch but have almost no moisture.
Crunchy foods.Jelly: A trap: it's a soft gel that wobbles instead of snapping, held in shape by pectin or gelatin.
Crunchy foods.Pudding: Smooth and creamy by design. It is thickened by starch or eggs, with nothing to crunch against.
Crunchy foods.Mashed potato: Cooked potatoes are mashed until soft, so no crunch at all. Overworking them releases starch and makes them gluey.
Crunchy foods.Yogurt: Yogurt is soft and smooth, so it's no crunch food, though it's often paired with granola for contrast.
Crunchy foods.Soup: Liquid food has no crunch, which is why chefs add croutons or crispy toppings for contrast.
Crunchy foods.Custard: Custard is a smooth, wobbly mix of milk and eggs. Only when its sugar is burned into crème brûlée's top does it crack.
Crunchy foods.Banana: Banana is soft and creamy, but freeze-dried banana chips are crunchy, which makes this a tricky case.
Crunchy foods.Oatmeal: Oatmeal is softened by cooking, though raw oats are chewy and toasted ones, as in granola, crunch.
Crunchy foods.Mousse: Mousse is designed to be airy and soft, with whipped cream or egg whites folded in. It's the opposite of crunchy.
Crunchy foods.Hummus: A smooth dip of chickpeas and tahini. Chickpeas are hard when dry, but cooking and blending takes the crunch out.
Crunchy foods.Marshmallow: Marshmallows are soft and spongy, though toasting one over a fire gives it a crisp, caramelized crust.

Insects that sting.Honeybee: A honeybee's barbed stinger stays in the skin and tears free, so a sting is fatal for the bee.
Insects that sting.Wasp: Unlike honeybees, wasps can sting repeatedly because their stingers are smooth and don't stay stuck in skin.
Insects that sting.Hornet: The Asian giant hornet has a sting delivering venom strong enough that victims describe it as like a hot nail.
Insects that sting.Yellowjacket: A yellowjacket is a wasp, not a bee, and it often becomes aggressive in late summer as colonies run low on food.
Insects that sting.Fire ant: Its sting burns like fire, hence the name, and colonies can form floating rafts to survive floods.
Insects that sting.Bullet ant: It is said to deliver the most painful insect sting; the pain is compared to being shot, hence the name, and it can last for a day.
Insects that sting.Bumblebee: Bumblebees can sting repeatedly, but they are gentle and rarely do so unless handled.
Insects that sting.Velvet ant: A trap: it's actually a wingless wasp covered in fuzzy hair, and its sting is so painful it's nicknamed cow killer.
Insects that sting.Paper wasp: These wasps chew wood into pulp to build the papery nest, and they can sting more than once.
Insects that sting.Mosquito: It bites with a needle-like mouth to draw blood rather than stinging with a venomous tail.
Insects that sting.Horsefly: Females slice skin with scissor-like mouthparts to feed on blood; it bites rather than stings.
Insects that sting.Flea: A flea bites with a piercing mouth, not a stinger, and it can jump about 100 times its length.
Insects that sting.Bed bug: A bed bug bites to feed on blood; it has no stinger.
Insects that sting.Tick: Ticks are arachnids that bite and attach themselves, and they don't sting.
Insects that sting.Scorpion: A trap: scorpions sting, with a venomous tail, but they are arachnids, not insects.
Insects that sting.Stingray: Its barbed tail does sting, but it's a fish, not an insect.
Insects that sting.Jellyfish: Its tentacles sting, but it's a sea animal, not an insect, and it has no brain.
Insects that sting.Spider: Spiders bite with fangs rather than stinging, and are arachnids, not insects.
Insects that sting.Ladybug: Harmless to people; it protects itself by releasing foul-tasting fluid rather than stinging.
Insects that sting.Butterfly: It cannot sting at all, and its wings' bright colors warn predators it tastes bad.
Insects that sting.Dragonfly: Harmless to people, with no stinger; it is an ace hunter that eats mosquitoes.
Insects that sting.Moth: Moths have no stinger, though the hairs on some caterpillars can irritate skin.
Insects that sting.Cockroach: Cockroaches don't sting or bite much; they're famous for surviving without a head for a week.
Insects that sting.Termite: Termites have no stinger, but they build mounds with their own air conditioning that can tower over 8 meters.

Indian dishes.Biryani: Layered rice and spiced meat, sealed and slow-cooked; Hyderabad, Lucknow and Kolkata each claim their own version.
Indian dishes.Butter chicken: Invented in Delhi in the 1950s when cooks mixed leftover tandoori chicken into a tomato and butter sauce.
Indian dishes.Dal: A staple lentil stew across India, and in some households there is a different dal served nearly every day.
Indian dishes.Samosa: Despite being a classic Indian snack, the triangular pastry has Central Asian and Middle Eastern ancestors.
Indian dishes.Dosa: A thin, crisp pancake from southern India, made from fermented rice and lentil batter; some are as long as a metre.
Indian dishes.Idli: Soft steamed cakes of fermented rice and lentil batter, a South Indian breakfast that is light and very low in fat.
Indian dishes.Palak paneer: Cubes of fresh cheese in a spinach gravy; paneer is made by curdling milk with acid and does not melt when heated.
Indian dishes.Chana masala: Spiced chickpeas simmered in a tangy tomato gravy, often eaten with bhature or puri in northern India.
Indian dishes.Rogan josh: A Kashmiri lamb curry whose red colour comes from dried Kashmiri chilies and the plant alkanet, not from a great deal of heat.
Indian dishes.Vindaloo: The name comes from the Portuguese 'vinha d'alhos' (wine and garlic), as the dish originated in Goa under Portuguese rule.
Indian dishes.Tandoori chicken: Chicken marinated in yoghurt and spices and cooked at very high heat in a clay oven called a tandoor.
Indian dishes.Korma: A mild, creamy braise from Mughal cuisine, whose name comes from a word for 'braise' and which uses yoghurt and nuts.
Indian dishes.Pav bhaji: A spicy mashed vegetable curry served with buttered bread rolls, invented in Mumbai as a quick meal for textile mill workers.
Indian dishes.Gulab jamun: Milk-solid dumplings fried and soaked in rose syrup; the name comes from Persian words for rosewater and a fruit.
Indian dishes.Rendang: Indonesian slow-cooked beef curry from the Minangkabau people, so it isn't from India.
Indian dishes.Laksa: Malaysian and Singaporean spicy noodle soup, not Indian.
Indian dishes.Pad thai: Thai stir-fried rice noodles with tamarind and peanuts, so not Indian, though both cuisines love tamarind.
Indian dishes.Shawarma: A Middle Eastern dish of meat shaved from a rotating spit, not Indian.
Indian dishes.Falafel: Middle Eastern chickpea or fava bean fritters, not Indian.
Indian dishes.Hummus: A Levantine dip made from chickpeas and tahini, so it doesn't fit, though chickpeas are also popular in India.
Indian dishes.Pho: Vietnamese noodle soup with a long-simmered beef broth, so not Indian, and often eaten for breakfast in Hanoi.
Indian dishes.Jollof rice: West African rice dish whose origins are fiercely debated between Nigeria and Ghana, and not Indian.
Indian dishes.Bibimbap: A Korean dish of mixed rice, not Indian.
Indian dishes.Tagine: A North African stew named for the conical clay pot it is cooked in, so it isn't Indian.

Italian desserts.Tiramisu: The name means 'pick me up'; layers of coffee-soaked sponge fingers and mascarpone, with a disputed origin in Veneto or Friuli.
Italian desserts.Panna cotta: The name means 'cooked cream'; a Piedmont dessert set lightly with gelatin so that it wobbles when turned out.
Italian desserts.Cannoli: Crisp fried shells filled with sweet ricotta, from Sicily; 'cannoli' is the plural, and one is a 'cannolo'.
Italian desserts.Gelato: Italian ice cream is churned slower than other ice creams and has less air and fat, so the flavours taste intense.
Italian desserts.Biscotti: Their name means 'twice-baked', which makes them hard and long-lasting, ideal for dunking in sweet wine or coffee.
Italian desserts.Zabaglione: A light, frothy custard of whisked egg yolks, sugar and Marsala wine, which is whisked over gentle heat.
Italian desserts.Affogato: The name means 'drowned': a scoop of gelato 'drowned' in a shot of hot espresso.
Italian desserts.Panettone: A tall, airy Christmas bread from Milan, with candied fruit, and it takes days to make because of its long rising.
Italian desserts.Sfogliatella: A shell-shaped pastry from Naples whose many thin layers resemble leaves; the name means 'small leaf'.
Italian desserts.Semifreddo: The name means 'half cold'; it's a partially frozen dessert of whipped cream and eggs, with a mousse-like texture.
Italian desserts.Granita: A Sicilian semi-frozen dessert of crushed ice and flavour, traditionally eaten for breakfast with a brioche.
Italian desserts.Pandoro: The Verona Christmas cake whose name means 'golden bread', baked in an eight-pointed star mould.
Italian desserts.Cassata: A Sicilian sponge cake with ricotta and candied fruit, covered in marzipan, whose name may derive from Arabic.
Italian desserts.Crème brûlée: A French custard with a caramelised sugar top, not Italian.
Italian desserts.Churros: Spanish fried dough sticks, usually dunked in thick hot chocolate, so not Italian.
Italian desserts.Baklava: Layers of nuts and syrup-soaked filo from the Ottoman world, not Italian.
Italian desserts.Flan: A caramel custard from Spain and Latin America, not Italian, though similar to panna cotta.
Italian desserts.Strudel: An Austrian pastry of thin dough around fruit, though it is popular in South Tyrol, in northern Italy, it's not an Italian classic.
Italian desserts.Éclair: A French choux pastry filled with cream, not Italian.
Italian desserts.Macaron: A French almond meringue sandwich, not Italian, though it is sometimes claimed to have come from Italy.
Italian desserts.Trifle: A British layered dessert, not Italian, although it is sometimes called 'zuppa inglese' in Italy.
Italian desserts.Pavlova: A meringue dessert claimed by Australia and New Zealand, not Italian.
Italian desserts.Brownie: An American chocolate baked bar, not Italian.
Italian desserts.Mochi: Chewy Japanese rice cakes, pounded from glutinous rice, so not Italian, and they cause a few choking accidents each New Year.

US states that border Canada.Idaho: Borders British Columbia in a small northern slice. Known for potatoes, with a license plate that says 'Famous Potatoes'.
US states that border Canada.Montana: Borders three Canadian provinces, more than any other state, and includes Glacier National Park, which is shared with Canada.
US states that border Canada.North Dakota: Home to the geographic centre of North America, near Rugby, and it shares a long border with Canada with its own peace garden.
US states that border Canada.Minnesota: Its northern border includes the Northwest Angle, the only part of the contiguous US north of the 49th parallel, reached by land only through Canada.
US states that border Canada.New York: Borders Canada at Niagara Falls, and across Lake Ontario. The falls are shared with Ontario.
US states that border Canada.Vermont: Borders Quebec, and its capital Montpelier is the smallest state capital by population in the US.
US states that border Canada.New Hampshire: Touches Quebec along a short northern border. It was the first colony to declare independence from Britain, in January 1776.
US states that border Canada.Maine: The easternmost state of the contiguous US borders New Brunswick and Quebec. It is the only US state that borders just one other US state.
US states that border Canada.Alaska: Borders Canada's Yukon and British Columbia, and was bought from Russia in 1867 for about 2 cents an acre.
US states that border Canada.Oregon: A trap: it neighbours Washington to the south, but its northern border is a Washington state line, not Canada.
US states that border Canada.Wyoming: A trap: home of Yellowstone, but Montana lies between it and Canada, so it has no Canadian border.
US states that border Canada.South Dakota: North Dakota is the neighbour that borders Canada. South Dakota, home of Mount Rushmore, doesn't.
US states that border Canada.Iowa: A trap: it sits in the Midwest with Minnesota to its north, so it does not touch Canada.
US states that border Canada.Massachusetts: A trap: in New England, but Vermont and New Hampshire sit between it and Canada.
US states that border Canada.Connecticut: A trap: a small southern New England state with no Canadian border; New York and Massachusetts lie to the north.
US states that border Canada.Nevada: A trap: home of Las Vegas, but Oregon and Idaho lie between it and the Canadian border.
US states that border Canada.Utah: A trap: Zion and Arches are far from Canada, with Idaho and Wyoming lying in between.
US states that border Canada.Colorado: A trap: a Rocky Mountain state with dozens of peaks over 14,000 feet, but nowhere near Canada.
US states that border Canada.Nebraska: A trap: a Great Plains state in the middle of the country, with South Dakota between it and Canada.
US states that border Canada.Rhode Island: A trap: the smallest US state, in New England, nowhere near Canada.
US states that border Canada.Hawaii: A trap: a chain of Pacific islands about 3,800 km from the mainland, so no land border at all.
US states that border Canada.Illinois: A trap: it touches Lake Michigan but no Canadian waters, unlike Michigan or Ohio, which share the Great Lakes border.
US states that border Canada.Kansas: A trap: near the geographic centre of the lower 48, far south of the Canadian border.

Landmarks in Paris.Eiffel Tower: Built for the 1889 World's Fair and meant to stand only 20 years, it survived because its height made it a useful radio antenna.
Landmarks in Paris.Louvre: A medieval fortress turned royal palace, it is the most visited museum on Earth, and its glass pyramid entrance opened in 1989.
Landmarks in Paris.Notre-Dame: The medieval cathedral on Île de la Cité was badly damaged by the 2019 fire and reopened to visitors in December 2024.
Landmarks in Paris.Arc de Triomphe: Napoleon ordered it in 1806 to honor his army, but it was finished only in 1836. It now shelters the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
Landmarks in Paris.Sacré-Cœur: This white basilica crowns Montmartre, the city's highest hill. Its travertine stone secretes calcite, so it stays white even in the rain.
Landmarks in Paris.Champs-Élysées: The name means Elysian Fields, the Greek paradise for heroes. The avenue runs from Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe.
Landmarks in Paris.Moulin Rouge: This cabaret with a red windmill opened in 1889 and helped popularize the can-can. Toulouse-Lautrec's posters made it famous.
Landmarks in Paris.Montmartre: Picasso, Modigliani and Van Gogh all lived around this hilltop village, and painters still crowd its Place du Tertre today.
Landmarks in Paris.Seine: The river runs about 775 km from Burgundy to the English Channel, and its banks through central Paris are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Landmarks in Paris.Musée d'Orsay: Housed in a grand railway station built for the 1900 Exposition, it now holds the world's finest Impressionist paintings.
Landmarks in Paris.Big Ben: London, not Paris. Strictly, the name belongs to the huge bell inside the Elizabeth Tower, not to the clock tower itself.
Landmarks in Paris.Colosseum: Rome's amphitheater opened in AD 80 and could seat around 50,000 spectators, but it stands in Italy, not France.
Landmarks in Paris.Sagrada Família: Gaudí's Barcelona basilica has been under construction since 1882. He died in 1926 with it far from finished.
Landmarks in Paris.Brandenburg Gate: Berlin's neoclassical gate dates from 1791. It sat beside the Berlin Wall and became a symbol of German reunification.
Landmarks in Paris.Trevi Fountain: Rome's Baroque fountain collects coins tossed over the shoulder, worth over a million euros a year, which go to charity.
Landmarks in Paris.Acropolis: Athens's hilltop citadel, crowned by the Parthenon. Its Greek name simply means high city.
Landmarks in Paris.Buckingham Palace: London's royal residence has 775 rooms, including 78 bathrooms. Paris has no equivalent royal home in town.
Landmarks in Paris.Leaning Tower: Pisa's bell tower began to tilt while still being built, because of soft ground, and it took about 200 years to finish.
Landmarks in Paris.Atomium: Brussels' shiny landmark from the 1958 World's Fair is an iron crystal cell enlarged about 165 billion times.
Landmarks in Paris.Mont Saint-Michel: This abbey on a tidal island in Normandy is cut off by some of Europe's highest tides, but it is far from Paris.
Landmarks in Paris.Versailles: A trap. This palace is famous and French, but it lies in a town about 20 km southwest of Paris, not within the city.
Landmarks in Paris.Little Mermaid: Copenhagen's small bronze statue from 1913 honors Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale, and it has been beheaded more than once.
Landmarks in Paris.Tower Bridge: London's bridge, often mistaken for the plainer London Bridge upstream, still lifts its roadway for tall ships.
Landmarks in Paris.Manneken Pis: Brussels' tiny fountain statue of a urinating boy owns hundreds of costumes, which he is dressed in on special occasions.

Places named after a person.Washington: Both the state and the capital honor George Washington, and the state is the only one named for a president.
Places named after a person.Bolivia: It was named for Simon Bolivar, the Venezuelan liberator who helped free much of South America from Spain.
Places named after a person.Colombia: The country honors Christopher Columbus, though he never reached its mainland, and it was named by 19th-century independence leaders.
Places named after a person.Philippines: Named in 1540s for Philip II of Spain, whose reign later included its colonization.
Places named after a person.Saudi Arabia: It is named for the House of Saud, the ruling dynasty, and it is among a small number of countries named for a family.
Places named after a person.Houston: The Texas city is named for Sam Houston, who led the army that won independence from Mexico.
Places named after a person.Seattle: It honors Chief Si'ahl, a Duwamish and Suquamish leader who was friendly with early settlers, and the city's name anglicizes his.
Places named after a person.Vancouver: The Canadian city is named for Captain George Vancouver, who explored this coast in 1792.
Places named after a person.Alexandria: Alexander the Great founded this Egyptian city in 331 BC, and its famed lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders.
Places named after a person.Pennsylvania: It means Penn's woods, named in honor of Admiral William Penn, the father of the colony's founder.
Places named after a person.Darwin: The Australian city is named for Charles Darwin, after the ship Beagle visited the harbor in 1839.
Places named after a person.Melbourne: It is named for Lord Melbourne, who was British prime minister in 1837, and the Australian city is a capital of culture.
Places named after a person.Iceland: Trap: its name is from the ice and the island, supposedly given by a Viking, Floki, who was unhappy with it.
Places named after a person.Argentina: Trap: it comes from the Latin argentum, silver, a hope from early explorers that it was full of the metal.
Places named after a person.Ecuador: Trap: its name is Spanish for the equator, which crosses the country.
Places named after a person.Costa Rica: Trap: its name means rich coast, a hopeful label from Spanish explorers.
Places named after a person.Honduras: Trap: its name means depths, perhaps referring to deep waters off the coast.
Places named after a person.Montenegro: Trap: it means black mountain, in Venetian, for its dark forested peaks.
Places named after a person.Nevada: Trap: Spanish for snow-covered, after the Sierra Nevada mountains.
Places named after a person.Florida: Trap: it is from the Spanish for flowery, and was named by Ponce de Leon during the Easter season of 1513.
Places named after a person.Tokyo: Trap: its name means eastern capital, and it was originally known as Edo.
Places named after a person.Canada: Trap: from the Iroquoian word kanata, meaning village or settlement.
Places named after a person.Chicago: Trap: it comes from an Algonquian word that probably referred to wild leeks or onions growing there.
Places named after a person.Toronto: Trap: this city's name is likely from a Mohawk word meaning where trees stand in the water.

Found in Antarctica.Penguins: Emperor penguins breed in Antarctic winter, and the males huddle through darkness and blizzards, balancing a single egg on their feet for about two months.
Found in Antarctica.South Pole: Sits on an ice cap nearly 3 kilometres thick. The Amundsen-Scott station there is occupied year-round, and the sun rises and sets only once a year.
Found in Antarctica.McMurdo Station: The largest research base on the continent, run by the United States, can house over 1,000 people in summer and it sits on Ross Island.
Found in Antarctica.Mount Erebus: The southernmost active volcano on Earth contains a permanent lava lake. It was named after a Royal Navy ship used in a 19th-century expedition.
Found in Antarctica.Ross Ice Shelf: The world's largest ice shelf is roughly the size of France, and its towering cliff edge faces the Ross Sea.
Found in Antarctica.Vinson Massif: At about 4,892 metres, this is the continent's highest peak. It was only discovered in 1957 and first climbed in 1966.
Found in Antarctica.Leopard seals: Fearsome Antarctic predators growing up to 3 metres long, they ambush penguins at the ice edge and also eat krill and other seals.
Found in Antarctica.Krill: These tiny shrimp-like crustaceans form swarms so dense they're visible from space, and they feed whales, seals and penguins across the Southern Ocean.
Found in Antarctica.Weddell Sea: Named after British sealer James Weddell, this sea has some of the clearest water on Earth. Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed by its ice in 1915.
Found in Antarctica.Lake Vostok: A huge freshwater lake buried beneath about 4 kilometres of Antarctic ice, sealed off for millions of years and drilled into by Russian scientists.
Found in Antarctica.Polar bears: A classic trap, since they live only in the Arctic. Their name even comes from the north, and penguins live at the opposite end of the planet.
Found in Antarctica.Arctic foxes: Despite sharing the poles' cold, they roam the northern tundra only. Antarctica has no land mammals native to it at all.
Found in Antarctica.Walruses: These tusked giants live around the Arctic Ocean, not the south. Antarctica's seals, such as the elephant seal, are their closest southern counterparts.
Found in Antarctica.North Pole: Sits in the middle of the frozen Arctic Ocean, not on land. It is the opposite end of the planet from Antarctica, thousands of kilometres away.
Found in Antarctica.Reindeer: Native to the Arctic and sub-Arctic north. A few were introduced to South Georgia island, but they don't live on the Antarctic mainland.
Found in Antarctica.Svalbard: This Norwegian archipelago is in the Arctic Ocean, far from Antarctica, and it houses the Global Seed Vault.
Found in Antarctica.Greenland: The world's largest island lies in the north Atlantic and Arctic. Its ice sheet is second only to Antarctica's in size.
Found in Antarctica.Igloos: These snow shelters belong to the Inuit of the Arctic. Antarctica never had an indigenous human population, so no one ever built them there.
Found in Antarctica.Narwhals: The unicorn whales with a long tusk live in Arctic waters near Greenland and Canada, not Antarctica.
Found in Antarctica.Musk oxen: Shaggy survivors of the ice age, they live in the Arctic tundra of Canada, Greenland and Alaska, never Antarctica.
Found in Antarctica.Lemmings: Small Arctic rodents, famously and wrongly said to leap off cliffs in mass suicide. They don't live anywhere near Antarctica.
Found in Antarctica.Puffins: These colourful seabirds nest in the North Atlantic and Pacific. Penguins fill a similar niche in the south, though they're unrelated.
Found in Antarctica.Snowy owls: These white hunters breed on the Arctic tundra and wander south in winter, but they've never been in Antarctica.
Found in Antarctica.Moose: Moose roam northern forests of North America and Eurasia. There are none in Antarctica, where no land animal larger than an insect lives year round.

Things currently orbiting Earth.The Moon: It's Earth's only natural satellite, about a quarter of Earth's width, and it's drifting away from us by roughly 4 centimeters a year.
Things currently orbiting Earth.ISS: The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so its crew sees around 16 sunrises a day.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Hubble: The space telescope has orbited about 540 km up since 1990 and was repaired by astronauts several times.
Things currently orbiting Earth.GPS satellites: About thirty of these satellites orbit at roughly 20,000 km, and their clocks must account for relativity to stay accurate.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Space junk: Tens of thousands of tracked pieces, from dead satellites to paint flecks, travel at roughly 28,000 km/h, fast enough that a tiny fleck can dent a spacecraft.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Tiangong: China's space station, whose name means Heavenly Palace, has been crewed since 2022.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Starlink satellites: This growing mega-constellation already makes up a large share of all active satellites, and its trains of lights have startled stargazers.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Weather satellites: These watch clouds and storms from orbit, either circling the poles or parked high above one spot on the equator.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Spy satellites: Many are in low orbit and photograph the ground in sharp detail, and their exact capabilities are classified.
Things currently orbiting Earth.TV satellites: Geostationary ones sit about 36,000 km up over the equator, so a home dish can stay aimed at a single spot.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Mars: Mars orbits the Sun, not Earth, and its two small moons circle Mars instead.
Things currently orbiting Earth.The Sun: It's the star we orbit, not a satellite of ours, and light from it takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Venus: Venus has no moon at all, and it's one of the few planets without one. It circles the Sun, not us.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Voyager 1: It sits near a point about 1.5 million km from Earth, called L2, and circles the Sun with us, so it isn't in Earth orbit.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Halley's Comet: It orbits the Sun about every 76 years, and it was last close to Earth in 1986. It's not an Earth orbiter.
Things currently orbiting Earth.James Webb telescope: It sits at a point a million miles away from Earth, called L2, so it isn't circling the planet.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Pluto: Pluto circles the Sun every 248 years, far from Earth, and reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Mir: The Russian space station was brought down in 2001 and burned up over the Pacific, so it's no longer in orbit.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Skylab: America's first space station fell to Earth in 1979, scattering debris over Western Australia.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Europa: One of Jupiter's moons, with an ocean under its ice, and it's nowhere near Earth.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Ceres: The largest object in the asteroid belt, and a dwarf planet, which orbits the Sun, not Earth.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Phobos: One of Mars's two small moons, it's slowly spiraling inward and will break apart in tens of millions of years.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Asteroid belt: A huge region of rocks between Mars and Jupiter, which orbit the Sun, not Earth.
Things currently orbiting Earth.Sputnik 1: The first artificial satellite, launched in 1957 by the Soviet Union, it fell back to Earth within three months.

Characters from Friends.Monica Geller: The group's perfectionist chef and cleaning fanatic. Courteney Cox reportedly auditioned for Rachel first, then asked to play Monica instead.

Characters from Friends.Ross Geller: The dinosaur-loving paleontologist is married three times over the series, a running gag that David Schwimmer's Ross never lives down.
Characters from Friends.Gunther: The Central Perk manager secretly loved Rachel for years. James Michael Tyler started as a background extra and was later given a speaking role.
Characters from Friends.Janice: Maggie Wheeler's Janice, with her nasal 'Oh. My. God!' and honking laugh, kept reappearing across all ten seasons as Chandler's on-and-off girlfriend.

Things that buzz.Bee: A honeybee's wings beat roughly 200 times a second, and that's the buzz you hear.
Things that buzz.Mosquito: Only females bite; the whine is their wingbeat, and males home in on its pitch.
Things that buzz.Fly: A housefly's wings beat about 200 times a second, which makes it a classic buzzer.
Things that buzz.Wasp: Most wasps are predators, feeding chewed insects to their grubs rather than pollen.
Things that buzz.Electric razor: The Schick electric razor reached shops in 1931, and its motor hasn't stopped buzzing since.
Things that buzz.Kazoo: You hum into it and a thin membrane adds the buzz, so it isn't blown like a flute.
Things that buzz.Hornet: Hornets are the largest social wasps, and their buzz is typically deeper.
Things that buzz.Bumblebee: Bumblebees can buzz-pollinate, shaking pollen loose from tomatoes and blueberries by vibrating flowers.
Things that buzz.Game show buzzer: On Jeopardy!, ringing in before the clue is read locks the buzzer out for a moment, so rushing costs time.
Things that buzz.Neon sign: The hum comes from the transformer and gas tube, and neon itself glows red-orange.
Things that buzz.Cicada: Males of some species rank among the loudest insects, and periodic ones emerge after 13 or 17 years.
Things that buzz.Phone on vibrate: A tiny motor with an off-centre weight shakes the phone to make that buzz.
Things that buzz.Butterfly: Butterflies flutter in near silence, since their big wings beat slowly.
Things that buzz.Ant: Ants are silent to us, though they communicate through chemicals and vibrations.
Things that buzz.Spider: Spiders make no buzz; their senses rely on vibrations in webs and on their legs.
Things that buzz.Snail: Snails glide silently on a layer of mucus.
Things that buzz.Worm: Worms are mute, though heavy rain can bring them to the surface.
Things that buzz.Caterpillar: Caterpillars move silently, though some species can click or squeak when threatened.
Things that buzz.Owl: Owls hoot, but their feathers are fringed so they fly in near silence.
Things that buzz.Cat: Cats purr, a low rumble of about 25 vibrations a second rather than a buzz.
Things that buzz.Feather: A feather falls without a sound, and its barbs let birds fly quietly.
Things that buzz.Cloud: Clouds drift silently; thunder is the noise nearby.
Things that buzz.Snake: Snakes hiss, and rattlesnakes rattle, but a true buzz isn't their sound.
Things that buzz.Goldfish: Goldfish are silent, yet they hear very well.

Things that crunch.Celery: Celery is about 95 percent water, and its crunch comes from stringy fibres snapping.
Things that crunch.Potato chips: A 2008 Ig Nobel-winning study showed that louder crunches make chips taste fresher to listeners.
Things that crunch.Dry leaves: Dry leaves crunch because brittle cell walls snap underfoot.
Things that crunch.Fresh snow: Fresh snow squeaks and crunches as ice crystals crush and break, especially in the cold.
Things that crunch.Gravel: Gravel crunches because stones grind and shift against each other.
Things that crunch.Toast: Toast's crunch comes from water driven out and sugars browning into crisp, brittle crumbs.
Things that crunch.Carrot: A carrot's crunch is a crisp snap of water-filled cells, and carrots were once mostly purple or yellow.
Things that crunch.Cornflakes: The Kellogg brothers invented flaked cereal around 1894 when they accidentally left cooked wheat sitting.
Things that crunch.Apple: About a quarter of an apple is air, which is why apples float.
Things that crunch.Pretzel: Pretzels are boiled briefly in lye or baking soda before baking to get their dark crust.
Things that crunch.Croutons: Croutons are toasted bread cubes, invented to use stale bread.
Things that crunch.Jelly: Jelly wobbles because gelatin traps water in a mesh of protein strands, which is why it has no crunch at all.
Things that crunch.Pudding: Pudding is soft and smooth, built from milk thickened with starch or eggs, so it fails the crunch test completely.
Things that crunch.Soup: Soup is mostly liquid, but add croutons or crackers and you introduce the crunch yourself.
Things that crunch.Yogurt: Yogurt is milk thickened by bacteria into a smooth set, so any crunch has to come from granola on top.
Things that crunch.Mashed potato: Mashed potato is deliberately beaten smooth, which is why a crunch in it usually means something went wrong.
Things that crunch.Ice cream: Ice cream is silky because of tiny ice crystals; if you hear a crunch, it has probably partly melted and refrozen.
Things that crunch.Banana: Bananas are soft, and mildly radioactive from potassium-40, but still harmless in normal amounts.
Things that crunch.Marshmallow: Marshmallows were once made from the sap of the marsh mallow plant, and today's are spongy sugar and gelatin foam.
Things that crunch.Custard: Custard thickens when eggs set gently with heat; heat it too much and it curdles instead of crisping up.
Things that crunch.Honey: Honey can last for thousands of years because it's so low in moisture, and it's a smooth syrup rather than a crunchy snack.
Things that crunch.Butter: Butter is mostly fat, so it spreads and melts rather than shattering; it only crunches inside a very flaky pastry.
Things that crunch.Pillow: A pillow cushions your head and dampens sound; the only crunch is the one you hear from foam or old feathers.
Things that crunch.Smoothie: A smoothie is fruit blended to liquid, so even a crunchy apple loses its crunch once it goes in the blender.

Team sports with 11+ players per side.Cricket: A cricket side has eleven players, but only two batters and a bowler plus a wicketkeeper take the main action. A Test match can last five days.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Field hockey: Field hockey teams have eleven players including a goalkeeper, and the ball is hit only with the flat face of the stick.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.American football: Eleven players per side are on the field at once, but teams swap whole squads of offense, defense and special teams.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Bandy: Bandy is like hockey on a football-sized ice rink, using a ball and 11 players a side. It's popular in Russia, Sweden and Finland.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Canadian football: With 12 players per side and a longer, wider field than the US game, Canadian football has only three downs.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Rugby union: Rugby union teams have 15 players, split into forwards and backs. Its roots go back to the legendary story of William Webb Ellis.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Rugby league: Rugby league has 13 players per side, fewer than rugby union's 15, and a play-the-ball after each tackle.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Gaelic football: Fifteen players a side play Gaelic football, where you can carry, bounce, kick or hand-pass the ball. It's Ireland's most popular sport.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Hurling: Hurling has 15 per side and is one of the world's fastest field games. The ball, a sliotar, can top 100 km/h.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Aussie rules: Each team fields 18 on an oval ground, and goals are worth six points while behinds score one.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Shinty: Shinty is a Scottish stick-and-ball game with 12 per side, and players may hit the ball in the air. It's related to Irish hurling.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Camogie: The women's version of hurling, camogie has 15 per side. It's named in Irish and grew from a 1904 founding.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Baseball: Nine players take the field at once, fewer than 11, so baseball doesn't qualify even though its roster is bigger.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Volleyball: Six players on each side of the net, so far below eleven; the sport was invented in 1895 as a gentler alternative to basketball.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Basketball: Five players per side, a very small team, and invented in 1891 by James Naismith using a peach basket.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Ice hockey: Six players are on the ice per side, including the goalie, so ice hockey sits far below 11.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Water polo: Seven players per side including the goalkeeper, and they tread water constantly without touching the pool bottom.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Handball: Seven per side, including the goalie, so it falls short, even though scores can reach 30 or more goals.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Netball: Netball teams use seven players, each restricted to certain zones, so it falls short of eleven.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Polo: Polo has four riders per side, and each rider usually needs several horses for fresh mounts over the match.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Ultimate frisbee: Seven per side, and the sport is self-refereed under a 'spirit of the game' principle. Too few for this list.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Rugby sevens: As the name hints, sevens teams field seven players, and matches are fast, with two seven-minute halves, so it doesn't fit.
Team sports with 11+ players per side.Futsal: Futsal is five-a-side football on a hard court with a smaller, low-bounce ball. It's popular among Brazilian stars' early training.

Things a real Viking could have packed.Axe: The everyday tool and common weapon of a Viking. Even poor warriors could afford one, which made it more common than a sword.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Shield: Round and wooden, often with an iron boss at center. Viking shields were light enough to carry in battle and mount on ships' rails.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Sword: A prized, often inherited weapon, with some blades carrying the Ulfberht name. Swords were costly, so only the wealthy could own one.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Spear: The most common Viking weapon, cheaper than a sword and versatile in battle or hunting. Many warriors carried one.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Wool cloak: Vikings wore thick wool in cold climates, fastened at the shoulder with a brooch. Wool stays warm even when damp.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Drinking horn: Made from a cow's horn, often rimmed in metal. Feasting hall tales feature plenty of mead and ale served in them.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Bone comb: Vikings cared about grooming, and combs of bone or antler are common finds. They also helped fight lice.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Dried fish: Stockfish, air-dried cod, kept for months and fueled voyages. Norway still exports it, and it's a traditional food today.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Leather boots: Footwear of turned leather, sewn inside out then flipped. They suited long walks and ship decks.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Iron knife: Every Viking carried one for eating, carving and work. The knife was a basic tool of daily life.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Silver coins: Vikings traded silver and weighed it, using coins and cut pieces as currency. Hoards across Scandinavia hold Arab coins from the east.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Horned helmet: A popular myth, thanks largely to nineteenth-century costume designers for Wagner's operas. No Viking helmets with horns have been found.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Potatoes: A New World crop brought to Europe in the 1500s. Vikings, who lived centuries earlier, never saw one.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Magnetic compass: This reached Europe from China around the 1100s, later than the Viking Age. Vikings steered by sun, stars and coastlines.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Tea bags: These arrived in the early 1900s, about a thousand years after the Vikings. Tea itself wasn't known in Scandinavia then.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Sunglasses: Modern sunglasses began in the 1900s. Some Arctic peoples had snow goggles, but Vikings did not use them.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Chocolate: A Mesoamerican food that reached Europe in the 1500s. Vikings had never tasted it, and no cacao grew in Scandinavia.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Gunpowder: Invented in China and reaching Europe only in the 1200s. Vikings fought with steel, not guns.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Tomatoes: A New World fruit that Europe adopted slowly after the 1500s. No Viking ever ate one, or even knew it existed.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Wristwatch: Wristwatches only became common in the late 1800s. Vikings told time by the sun, the stars and the seasons.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Telescope: Invented in the early 1600s in the Netherlands. Vikings navigated by sight and experience.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Matches: Friction matches date only to 1826. Vikings made fire using flint, steel and dry tinder, which they could carry.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Coffee: It reached Europe in the 1600s from the Middle East. Vikings had never tasted it and drank ale and mead instead.
Things a real Viking could have packed.Banknotes: Paper money came from China and spread later. Vikings valued metal, weighing silver rather than counting paper.

Invented in the 20th century.Television: Mechanical TV was shown in the 1920s, and Philo Farnsworth made the first all-electronic system in 1927, at just 21 years old.
Invented in the 20th century.Airplane: The Wright brothers' first powered flight in 1903 lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. Within 66 years, people walked on the Moon.
Invented in the 20th century.Internet: Its ancestor ARPANET sent its first message in 1969, and it crashed after two letters. The web was added by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
Invented in the 20th century.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket near radar equipment in 1945. The first ovens were as tall as a refrigerator.
Invented in the 20th century.Transistor: Invented at Bell Labs in 1947, it replaced bulky vacuum tubes. Modern chips hold billions of them.
Invented in the 20th century.Laser: Theodore Maiman built the first working one in 1960. Its name stands for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.
Invented in the 20th century.Ballpoint pen: Laszlo Biro, a Hungarian, patented his practical version in 1938. Its quick-drying ink made it far less messy than fountain pens.
Invented in the 20th century.Velcro: Swiss engineer George de Mestral invented it in the 1940s after burrs stuck to his dog's fur. He studied them under a microscope.
Invented in the 20th century.Jet engine: Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany developed it independently in the 1930s. The first jet flew in 1939.
Invented in the 20th century.Video game: Early ones like Tennis for Two appeared in 1958. Pong, in 1972, made the format a household name.
Invented in the 20th century.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876. It falls in the 19th century, so it doesn't fit.
Invented in the 20th century.Light bulb: Edison's practical bulb dates to 1879, so it is a 19th century invention. Others, such as Swan, worked on it too.
Invented in the 20th century.Steam engine: Newcomen built a working one in 1712, and Watt improved it in the 1760s. It powered the Industrial Revolution, well before the 1900s.
Invented in the 20th century.Printing press: Gutenberg's press arrived around 1450. It is among the most important inventions of the 15th century.
Invented in the 20th century.Telescope: Dutch lens makers patented one in 1608, and Galileo improved it the next year. It dates to the early 1600s.
Invented in the 20th century.Photography: Nicephore Niepce took the earliest surviving photo in the 1820s. It came a century before the 20th.
Invented in the 20th century.Telegraph: Samuel Morse's system was demonstrated in the 1830s and 1840s. It sped messages from days to minutes in the 1800s.
Invented in the 20th century.Bicycle: The pedal bicycle came in the 1860s, and the chain-driven safety bicycle in the 1880s. Both are 19th century.
Invented in the 20th century.Typewriter: The first commercially successful one, the Sholes and Glidden, appeared in 1873. The QWERTY layout dates from it.
Invented in the 20th century.Gunpowder: Invented in China over a thousand years ago, and one of the Four Great Inventions. It is far older than the 1900s.
Invented in the 20th century.Compass: Chinese navigators used magnetic compasses by roughly the 1100s. It's far older than the 1900s.
Invented in the 20th century.Stethoscope: Rene Laennec invented it in 1816, partly to avoid pressing his ear against a patient's chest. It's a 19th century device.
Invented in the 20th century.Dynamite: Alfred Nobel patented it in 1867, so it is a 19th century invention. His fortune from it funded the Nobel Prizes.
Invented in the 20th century.Sewing machine: Elias Howe patented a lockstitch version in 1846, and Isaac Singer made it a big success. Both are 19th century.

From Arthurian legend.Excalibur: Arthur's sword, which a lake spirit gave him; in some tellings he pulled it from the stone, in others it was a separate sword.
From Arthurian legend.Camelot: Arthur's court is first named by the French poet Chretien de Troyes in the 1100s, not in earlier Welsh sources.
From Arthurian legend.Merlin: The wizard first appeared in Geoffrey of Monmouth's 1100s writings, drawing on a Welsh bard named Myrddin.
From Arthurian legend.Lancelot: The greatest knight, whose affair with Guinevere helped bring down Camelot; he first shows up in Chretien de Troyes's romances.
From Arthurian legend.Guinevere: Arthur's queen, whose love for Lancelot splits the Round Table; her name comes from a Welsh word for 'white phantom'.
From Arthurian legend.Holy Grail: A sacred vessel; Galahad's quest for it is the central journey in the legend, and its meaning shifted from dish to chalice over time.
From Arthurian legend.Avalon: The mystic isle where Arthur's wounds were healed; some medieval writers equated it with Glastonbury.
From Arthurian legend.Round Table: A trap: Arthur's table that made all knights equal belongs to the Arthurian legend.
From Arthurian legend.Mordred: Arthur's traitorous nephew, or in some tellings, his son, who fights him at Camlann in the final battle.
From Arthurian legend.Lady of the Lake: The water spirit who gives Arthur Excalibur; in some tellings she is named Nimue, Vivien or Viviane.
From Arthurian legend.Morgan le Fay: Arthur's half-sister and an enchantress; once a healer in the early texts, she later became a villain.
From Arthurian legend.Galahad: The purest knight, son of Lancelot, who achieves the Grail; he is a latecomer in the legend, first appearing around 1200.
From Arthurian legend.Uther Pendragon: Arthur's father, who with Merlin's magic disguised himself as another man to sleep with Igraine, Arthur's mother.
From Arthurian legend.Sherwood Forest: The Nottinghamshire woodland of the ballads is real, and its Major Oak is said to be several centuries old.
From Arthurian legend.Robin Hood: A trap: the outlaw archer is a separate English legend, centered on Nottingham, with no Round Table link.
From Arthurian legend.Maid Marian: A trap: Robin Hood's love belongs to Sherwood, not Camelot, and joined the legend through later May Day plays.
From Arthurian legend.Friar Tuck: A trap: the Merry Men's jolly friar is Robin Hood's, never part of Arthur's knights.
From Arthurian legend.Mjolnir: Thor's hammer is Norse; it appears in the Eddas, which never overlap with Arthur's Britain.
From Arthurian legend.Valhalla: A trap: Odin's hall for slain warriors is Norse myth, not Arthurian.
From Arthurian legend.Olympus: A trap: the Greek gods' home, about 2,900 metres high, isn't Arthurian.
From Arthurian legend.Beowulf: An Old English epic hero, who fought Grendel; he's from a Scandinavian-set poem, not Arthurian legend.
From Arthurian legend.Grendel: The monster of the Old English poem Beowulf, a descendant of Cain, and unrelated to Arthur's Britain.
From Arthurian legend.Ivanhoe: Walter Scott's 1819 novel set in medieval England, not Arthurian; it helped popularize Robin Hood's image as a Saxon hero.
From Arthurian legend.Durandal: A trap: Roland's unbreakable sword in the French Song of Roland, not Arthur's.

Ancient ruins located in Italy.Pompeii: Vesuvius buried it in AD 79, preserving graffiti, shops and even loaves of bread.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Colosseum: Opened in AD 80, it held an estimated 50,000 spectators and had a retractable awning.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Herculaneum: Also buried in AD 79, it preserved wood and even papyrus scrolls in a villa library.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Paestum: A Greek colony in southern Italy with three Doric temples that rank among the best preserved anywhere.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Roman Forum: The heart of ancient Rome held the Senate House, temples and triumphal arches.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Pantheon: Nearly 1,900 years on, its dome remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Ostia Antica: Rome's ancient port is so well preserved that it has an apartment block, a theater and public toilets.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Circus Maximus: The chariot-racing stadium could hold several hundred thousand people. Today it is a park.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Agrigento: The Valley of the Temples in Sicily is the remains of a Greek colony, with the Temple of Concordia.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Hadrian's Villa: The emperor's sprawling retreat at Tivoli copied buildings he had seen on his travels.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Palatine Hill: Said to be where Romulus founded Rome, and the source of the word palace.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Acropolis: Athens' hilltop citadel and its Parthenon lie in Greece, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Delphi: The oracle's sanctuary, where the priestess spoke for Apollo, is in Greece, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Knossos: The Minoan palace is on the Greek island of Crete, not in Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Petra: The rose-red rock city carved by the Nabataeans is in Jordan, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Hadrian's Wall: Named for the emperor who built it, it spans northern England, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Pont du Gard: This three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge is in southern France, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Carthage: Rome's great enemy stood on the coast of Tunisia, in North Africa, and Rome destroyed it in 146 BC.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Leptis Magna: A grand and well-preserved Roman city on the coast of Libya, but not in Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Baalbek: Its giant Roman temples, among the biggest ever built, stand in Lebanon, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Jerash: A well-preserved Roman provincial city in Jordan, not Italy.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Diocletian's Palace: The retirement palace of a Roman emperor stands in Split, Croatia.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Segovia Aqueduct: This Roman aqueduct, built without mortar, is in Spain, and still dominates the town.
Ancient ruins located in Italy.Ephesus: A great Greek and Roman city, but its ruins stand in Turkey, not Italy.

Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Nave: The long central hall where worshippers gather. The word comes from the Latin for 'ship', and the vaulted roof can look like an upturned hull.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Apse: A semicircular or polygonal recess at the church's eastern end, usually behind the altar, which often holds the sanctuary.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Transept: The arms crossing the nave, which give a cathedral its cross-shaped plan when seen from above.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Spire: A tall pointed tower top. Salisbury Cathedral's, at about 123 metres, is the tallest medieval church spire in Britain.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Crypt: An underground chamber beneath the church, often holding tombs or relics, and in many cathedrals the oldest surviving part.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Altar: The table at the focus of the church, and the cathedral's whole eastward layout was planned around it.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Choir: The part of the church reserved for singers and clergy, often with carved wooden stalls, sitting between the nave and the altar.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Cloister: A covered walkway around a courtyard, where monks walked and studied. It was usually attached to monastery cathedrals.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Flying buttress: These external arches carry the roof's outward thrust down to piers outside, letting builders open the walls to huge windows.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Gargoyle: Most were waterspouts that threw rain clear of the walls, and they usually took grotesque forms. Ones that don't spout water are called grotesques.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Rose window: The huge circular stained-glass window with radiating tracery. Notre-Dame's north rose is about 13 metres across and dates to the 1250s.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Chancel: The area around the altar, once separated by a screen, where clergy led the service. The word comes from Latin for 'lattice'.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Moat: Trap: a water-filled ditch to stop attackers is a castle feature, so a cathedral needs no such defense.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Portcullis: Trap: a heavy iron grate dropped to seal a castle gate. It is a defensive device, and it also appears on the UK's parliamentary badge.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Drawbridge: Trap: a bridge that can be raised to block a castle entrance. Cathedrals welcomed everyone, so none needed it.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Keep: Trap: the castle's strongest inner tower, the last refuge when a siege went badly. It's also called a donjon.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Barbican: Trap: a fortified outer gateway of a castle. London's Barbican takes its name from an old fortification outpost.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Bailey: Trap: the walled courtyard of a castle, home to stables, kitchens and workshops, and the origin of the Old Bailey's name.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Dungeon: Trap: the word likely comes from 'donjon', the castle's keep, so prisoners were held in its cellars, not in a cathedral.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Arrow slit: Trap: a narrow castle opening that lets archers shoot while giving attackers a tiny target. Cathedrals got big windows instead.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Ramparts: Trap: the defensive earth or stone banks of a castle, with walkways on top for defenders.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Curtain wall: Trap: the defensive wall linking a castle's towers. The term is now also used for glass walls in skyscrapers.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Motte: Trap: the earth mound on which early Norman castles were built, usually topped by a wooden tower. It is paired with a bailey.
Parts of a Gothic cathedral (not a castl.Postern gate: Trap: a small back door in a castle wall, used for sneaking in or out in a siege.

Types of kitchen knife.Chef's knife: Usually about 20 centimeters long, it's called the one blade a cook can't do without because it slices, dices and chops.
Types of kitchen knife.Bread knife: Its serrations grip the crust and saw through without squashing the soft crumb.
Types of kitchen knife.Paring knife: 'Pare' means to trim away the skin; the short blade is for peeling and delicate work in the hand.
Types of kitchen knife.Cleaver: The Chinese cleaver, caidao, is often used for delicate slicing, while heavier Western cleavers hack through bone.
Types of kitchen knife.Butter knife: Legend says Cardinal Richelieu had pointed dinner knives blunted in 17th-century France, and the rounded tip stuck.
Types of kitchen knife.Steak knife: Many steakhouse knives are serrated, but chefs argue a straight edge cuts cleaner without tearing.
Types of kitchen knife.Fillet knife: Its long, thin, flexible blade follows a fish's backbone to separate flesh from bone.
Types of kitchen knife.Santoku: Japanese for 'three virtues', usually read as slicing, dicing and mincing.
Types of kitchen knife.Carving knife: Long and slender, it slices cooked roasts and is traditionally paired with a carving fork.
Types of kitchen knife.Boning knife: A narrow, sometimes flexible blade lets cooks work around joints and bones.
Types of kitchen knife.Spatula: Not a knife: it flips rather than cuts, though a palette knife for icing blurs the line.
Types of kitchen knife.Ladle: No blade here; a bowl-shaped dipper has been used for cooking since prehistoric clay pots.
Types of kitchen knife.Whisk: Its looped wires beat air into cream and eggs, and over-whipped cream eventually turns into butter.
Types of kitchen knife.Tongs: Tongs come from Old English tange; they grip and turn but never cut.
Types of kitchen knife.Skewer: Pointed but it pierces rather than cuts; soaking wooden ones in water stops them burning on the grill.
Types of kitchen knife.Colander: From Latin colare, 'to strain', a bowl with holes for draining pasta.
Types of kitchen knife.Grater: Sharp but not a knife: it shreds with punched teeth, and the Microplane began as a woodworking rasp.
Types of kitchen knife.Pestle: Always paired with a mortar, this crushing duo is among the oldest kitchen tools, used since prehistory.
Types of kitchen knife.Rolling pin: French-style pins are tapered with no handles, giving bakers a better feel for the dough.
Types of kitchen knife.Sieve: Sifting flour through it adds air and removes lumps, but nothing is sliced.
Types of kitchen knife.Funnel: From Latin infundibulum, 'to pour in'; it guides liquid but cuts nothing.
Types of kitchen knife.Potato masher: Overworking potatoes with a blender releases starch and makes them gluey, which is why a masher is gentler.
Types of kitchen knife.Ice cream scoop: Alfred Cralle, a Black inventor, patented a mechanical ice cream scoop in 1897.
Types of kitchen knife.Melon baller: A sharp-edged scoop that carves tidy spheres but isn't really a knife; it also cores pears.

Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Sock: Socks are among the classic robot vacuum casualties; the brushes wind them up, and many owners have rescued socks from underneath.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Charger cable: Cables are a top robot-vacuum menace, because they wrap around the brush roll and can even drag the plugged-in device off a table.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Lego brick: Lego bricks are tough enough to survive a vacuum, but a small one can jam the brush or end up in the bin among the dust.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Hair tie: Elastic hair ties are almost designed to snag a vacuum's brush, where they stretch and coil like a spring until the motor stalls.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Earbud: Earbuds are small and light enough to be sucked in, and wireless ones left on the floor regularly end up in the dustbin.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Coin: Coins are heavy enough to rattle the brush, and many owners find them in the dustbin along with the lost-and-found.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Paper clip: A paper clip is a small thing that can jam the brush, and its springy wire can tangle with hair and threads already wrapped there.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Cat toy: Feather wands and small stuffed mice look like food to a robot vacuum, and cats sometimes ride the machines like a Roomba taxi.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Shoelace: Shoelaces, like strings and cords, are notorious for winding around the brush roll and stopping the machine in its tracks.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Pet hair: Pet hair is exactly what robot vacuums are built for, and a single dog can produce enough fur to fill the bin on every run.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Crumbs: Crumbs are the easy meal: a robot vacuum's side brush flicks them in from corners where a normal one often misses.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Rubber band: Rubber bands are nasty for brush rolls, and they can melt or stretch around the axle, so removing them is a chore.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Sofa: Most robot vacuums stand only a few inches tall, so a sofa is far too big to swallow, though they often slip underneath.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Dog: A dog won't be swallowed, though a robot vacuum can leave a mess when a pet has an accident, a famous disaster nicknamed 'poopocalypse'.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Fridge: A fridge is far too heavy and tall; a robot vacuum simply sees it as an obstacle and bumps around it with sensors.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Dining table: A dining table is an obstacle course of legs for a robot vacuum, but the tabletop itself is far out of reach.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Bookcase: Robot vacuums can't swallow bookcases, but the dust bunnies underneath one can be a feast if the gap is tall enough.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Double bed: A double bed is too big, though a robot vacuum can often slide beneath if the frame leaves a gap of a few inches.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Armchair: An armchair is an obstacle, not a snack, and robots map furniture with lasers or cameras to steer around it.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Piano: A piano weighs hundreds of pounds, so the robot vacuum just treats the legs as an obstacle and goes around them.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.TV stand: A low TV stand can actually trap a robot vacuum underneath, which is why many owners block the gap rather than risk a rescue.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Washing machine: A washing machine is far beyond a robot's size, though a robot can sometimes get wedged in the gap beside one.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Wardrobe: A wardrobe is too large to swallow, and its main danger to a robot vacuum is the dust bunnies hiding underneath.
Things a robot vacuum might swallow.Bathtub: A bathtub is simply a fixed obstacle, and most robot vacuums can't climb steps or edges higher than about an inch or two.

Things that inflate.Balloon: A balloon's latex stretches many times its size, and its rubber comes from rubber trees.
Things that inflate.Air mattress: An air mattress holds its shape from trapped air, and some can bear several hundred pounds.
Things that inflate.Beach ball: A beach ball is so light that it's mostly air, and it floats in water.
Things that inflate.Bouncy castle: A bouncy castle needs a constant blower, since it has small vents and deflates when the power stops.
Things that inflate.Bike tire: A bike tire's pressure can hit over 100 psi on road bikes, much more than a car tire.
Things that inflate.Pool float: A pool float is just a big air bladder, and the fun part is that it floats on water.
Things that inflate.Basketball: A basketball is pumped to about 8 psi, and when it's too flat it won't bounce well.
Things that inflate.Airbag: An airbag inflates in about 30 milliseconds, using a chemical reaction that makes nitrogen gas.
Things that inflate.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon rises when heated air inside is lighter than the cooler air around it.
Things that inflate.Pufferfish: A pufferfish inflates by gulping water, making it too big for predators to swallow, and its organs hold a deadly toxin.
Things that inflate.Inflatable boat: An inflatable boat can be rolled up small, and some of them cross oceans.
Things that inflate.Blood pressure cuff: A blood pressure cuff inflates to squeeze an artery, and then slowly lets go so the doctor can read your pressure.
Things that inflate.Bowling ball: A bowling ball is solid, and it's made of dense resin with no inflation.
Things that inflate.Golf ball: A golf ball is solid or layered rubber, with dimples that help it fly farther.
Things that inflate.Marble: A marble is solid glass, and cannot be inflated.
Things that inflate.Brick: A brick is dense fired clay, with nothing to fill.
Things that inflate.Sponge: A sponge is porous, but it soaks up liquids and doesn't inflate.
Things that inflate.Rock: A rock is solid, and there's no way to fill it with air.
Things that inflate.Pool noodle: A pool noodle is solid foam, so it floats without any air to pump in.
Things that inflate.Bean bag: A bean bag is filled with beans or beads, not air.
Things that inflate.Yoga mat: A yoga mat is flat foam or rubber, with nothing to pump.
Things that inflate.Kickboard: A kickboard is solid foam, so it floats without being filled.
Things that inflate.Cricket ball: A cricket ball is a cork core wrapped in leather, and it isn't inflated.
Things that inflate.Hockey puck: A hockey puck is a hard rubber disc and is frozen before games to reduce bounce.

Ways to pay at a shop.Cash: Cash is still very popular in places like Germany and Japan, even though card payments grow every year.
Ways to pay at a shop.Credit card: The Diners Club card, introduced in 1950, is often credited as the first general-purpose charge card.
Ways to pay at a shop.Debit card: A debit card takes money straight from your bank balance, so overspending can trigger overdraft fees.
Ways to pay at a shop.Check: A check is a written order to your bank. It can take days to clear, and some shops no longer accept them.
Ways to pay at a shop.Bank transfer: A bank transfer moves money directly between accounts, which is common for rent and bigger purchases.
Ways to pay at a shop.PayPal: PayPal began in 1998 as Confinity and merged with Elon Musk's X.com in 2000, before eBay bought it in 2002.
Ways to pay at a shop.Apple Pay: Apple Pay launched in 2014 and uses a one-time token, so the shop never sees your real card number.
Ways to pay at a shop.Gift card: A gift card works like pre-loaded cash. Many go unspent, so stores quietly keep the leftover balance.
Ways to pay at a shop.Contactless: Contactless payments use short-range radio waves called NFC, which work only within a few centimeters of the reader.
Ways to pay at a shop.Google Pay: Google Pay stores a tokenized version of your card in your phone, so you can pay with a tap.
Ways to pay at a shop.Receipt: A receipt is proof that you paid, not a way to pay, which makes it a classic trap on this list.
Ways to pay at a shop.Invoice: An invoice asks for payment later, so it's a request for money rather than a method of paying.
Ways to pay at a shop.Price tag: A price tag only says what an item costs, and it can't settle the bill, so it isn't a way to pay.
Ways to pay at a shop.Barcode: A barcode identifies a product for the till, but it doesn't pay for anything, so it isn't a payment method.
Ways to pay at a shop.Shopping cart: The shopping cart was invented in 1937 by Sylvan Goldman in Oklahoma City, but it only holds goods, not payment.
Ways to pay at a shop.Cash register: James Ritty invented the cash register in 1879 to stop employees from pocketing money. It records payments but isn't one.
Ways to pay at a shop.Piggy bank: A piggy bank is for saving coins at home. A popular theory says the name comes from 'pygg', an old word for clay.
Ways to pay at a shop.Sales tax: Sales tax is added to a price, so you pay it with cash or card, and it isn't a way to pay in itself.
Ways to pay at a shop.Refund: A refund sends your money back, so it's payment going the opposite way, not a way of paying.
Ways to pay at a shop.ATM: The first ATM was installed at a Barclays branch in Enfield, London, in 1967. It dispenses cash but isn't a way to pay.
Ways to pay at a shop.Purse: A purse holds your cash and cards, but it's only the container, not a payment method itself.
Ways to pay at a shop.Budget: Budget comes from the French 'bougette', a small leather bag. It's a plan for spending, not a way to pay.
Ways to pay at a shop.Discount: A discount lowers the price, such as a sale or coupon. It changes how much you pay, not how you pay.
Ways to pay at a shop.Shopping list: A shopping list reminds you what to buy, but it plays no part in the paying itself, only in the planning.

Powers of two.2: The only even prime number, and the foundation of binary: every bit in a computer is a choice between two states.
Powers of two.4: Two plus two equals two times two, a coincidence that works only for this number; four bits also make a nibble.
Powers of two.8: Eight bits make a byte, the basic unit of computer memory, and it's also why an octave spans eight named notes.
Powers of two.10: Ten sits between 8 and 16, so it is no power of two, even though it is the base humans use to count.
Powers of two.16: One hexadecimal digit covers 0 to F, which is 16 values, so programmers love hex: each digit is exactly four bits.
Powers of two.24: 24-bit color gives 16.7 million shades, which is 2 to the 24th, but 24 itself is 3 x 8 and isn't a power of two.
Powers of two.32: 32-bit processors could address at most 4 GB of memory, a ceiling that drove the industry's move to 64-bit computing.
Powers of two.48: 48 kHz is a standard audio and video sampling rate, but 48 is 3 x 16, a near miss and not a power of two.
Powers of two.64: The Nintendo 64 got its name from its 64-bit processor, and the Commodore 64 from its 64 kilobytes of RAM.
Powers of two.96: 96 is 3 x 32, so it fails the test, though it appears in 96 kHz audio and plenty of computing contexts.
Powers of two.100: Though close to 128, a hundred isn't a power of two; it is a power of ten, which is how decimal people think.
Powers of two.120: 120 is a common screen refresh rate and divides by 8, but it is 15 x 8, so it is not itself a power of two.
Powers of two.128: Original ASCII defined exactly 128 characters using 7 bits, which is why old text files handle only basic English letters.
Powers of two.200: Two hundred sits between 128 and 256, so it is no power of two, though it fits comfortably within a single byte.
Powers of two.256: One byte can hold 256 different values, 0 to 255, which is why color channels in images typically top out at 255.
Powers of two.500: 500 is close to 512, which makes it a classic trap, but it is not a power of two; 512 is 2 to the 9th.
Powers of two.512: For decades 512 bytes was the standard disk sector size, and the number still lingers in storage and file system lore.
Powers of two.768: The screen size 1024 x 768 used 768, which is 3 x 256: close to a power of two, but multiplied by three.
Powers of two.1000: The metric kilo is exactly 1000, a near-miss of 1024, which is why a 1 TB drive appears as about 931 GB on many computers.
Powers of two.1024: Computing's 'kilo' once meant 1,024 rather than 1,000, so standards now call it a kibibyte to end the confusion.
Powers of two.1536: 1536 is 3 x 512 and equals 1.5 GB in memory terms, yet it isn't a power of two itself.
Powers of two.2048: Gabriele Cirulli built the sliding-tile game 2048 in a weekend in 2014, and it went viral almost overnight.
Powers of two.3000: 3000 sits between 2048 and 4096, so it is no power of two, even though it looks like a neat round number.
Powers of two.4096: The DCI 4K cinema standard is 4096 pixels wide, and 4096 is also 2 to the 12th power, a clean binary number.

Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Sunflowers: He painted several versions of these, and Gauguin admired them; the late-summer blooms were meant to decorate Gauguin's room in Arles.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Irises: Painted in 1889, these purple flowers were done in the Saint-Rémy asylum garden; the blue has faded over time.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Potato Eaters: His first major work, it shows a poor family eating by lamplight; he deliberately painted them with coarse, earthy tones.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Bedroom in Arles: He painted it in 1888 to feel restful, and made three versions of his simple room with its tilted perspective and blue walls.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Almond Blossoms: Painted in 1890 for his newborn nephew, this delicate branch of spring blossoms is one of his last works.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Sower: Millet's peasant theme inspired him; he painted this farmer against a huge yellow sun, in more than one version.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Night Café: Van Gogh said he tried to show that a café is a place where one can ruin oneself, using clashing reds and greens.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Yellow House: He rented this Arles house in 1888, hoping to build an artists' colony; Gauguin stayed there for two tense months.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Water Lilies: Monet painted around 250 of these pond scenes at Giverny, a very different Impressionist approach from Van Gogh's thick, swirling strokes.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Scream: Painted by Edvard Munch in 1893 after an anxious sunset walk; it is a Norwegian Expressionist icon.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Kiss: A golden Klimt masterpiece from 1907-08, it is one of Austria's best-loved paintings.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Guernica: Picasso's 1937 anti-war mural, painted after the bombing of a Basque town, is huge, in black, white and gray.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Mona Lisa: Leonardo da Vinci's portrait hangs in the Louvre and has been famous since it was stolen in 1911.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.American Gothic: Grant Wood painted this in 1930, using his sister and his dentist as models for the farmer and daughter.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Night Watch: Rembrandt's 1642 group portrait of a civic guard was once trimmed on the sides to fit a wall.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Nighthawks: Edward Hopper's 1942 diner scene of late-night loneliness is one of America's most-copied images.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Birth of Venus: Botticelli painted Venus rising on a shell around 1485, and it hangs in Florence's Uffizi.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Impression Sunrise: Monet's 1872 harbor scene at Le Havre gave Impressionism its name; he is not the painter here.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Son of Man: Magritte's 1964 portrait of a man with an apple in front of his face is Surreal, not Van Gogh.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Las Meninas: Velázquez painted this 1656 royal scene, in which the painter himself stands at an easel, in Madrid.

Painted by Vincent van Gogh.Christina's World: Andrew Wyeth's 1948 painting of a woman crawling in a field is a famed American picture, based on a neighbor with polio.
Painted by Vincent van Gogh.The Last Supper: Leonardo painted this around 1495-98 on a refectory wall in Milan, and it began flaking within decades.

Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Adèle Varens: Rochester's young French ward in Jane Eyre is the pupil Jane is hired to teach; Rochester says she may be the daughter of an opera dancer.
Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Helen Burns: Jane's saintly friend at Lowood school dies of consumption; Charlotte modelled her on her own sister Maria, who died young after a harsh boarding school.
Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Mr. Darcy: Pride and Prejudice is Jane Austen's work, not a Brontë one; his famous proud first proposal is rejected by Elizabeth Bennet.
Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Mr. Knightley: Emma's older friend and eventual husband belongs to Jane Austen's novel Emma, not to a Brontë book.

Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Elizabeth Bennet: Austen's witty heroine of Pride and Prejudice is a different world from the Brontës' stormy moors; Charlotte Brontë found Austen too tame.

Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Miss Havisham: Dickens's jilted bride, who stopped every clock at 8:40 and wore her wedding dress for decades, is a Great Expectations character.
Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Becky Sharp: Thackeray's scheming adventuress in Vanity Fair appeared in 1847-48, just as Jane Eyre did, but she belongs to Thackeray, not a Brontë.
Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Tess Durbeyfield: Thomas Hardy's tragic heroine in Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Hardy's creation, not a Brontë character.
Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Dorothea Brooke: Middlemarch's idealist is by George Eliot, a pen name; the Brontës also hid behind male names, as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.

Characters created by the Brontë sisters.Mrs. Danvers: The sinister housekeeper of Manderley comes from Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca, a gothic novel strongly influenced by Jane Eyre.
